questions.prompt: What problem do provide and inject solve?

options.text: Prop drilling — passing data through many intermediate components that don't use it

questions.explanation: provide/inject lets an ancestor share data directly with any descendant, avoiding the need to thread a prop through every layer in between.

questions.prompt: To share reactive state via provide, what should you provide?

options.text: The ref's unwrapped value, e.g. count.value
The ref (or reactive object) itself, e.g. count

questions.explanation: Provide the ref/reactive itself so injectors stay reactive. Providing count.value hands over a one-time snapshot that won't update.

questions.prompt: What is the second argument to inject(key, default) used for?

options.text: A default value used if no ancestor provided that key

questions.explanation: The optional second argument is a fallback value returned when the key wasn't provided anywhere up the tree.

questions.prompt: For type-safe injection in TypeScript, use an Injection______ (a typed Symbol) as the key. (one word)
questions.explanation: An InjectionKey<T> is a Symbol typed to carry the value's type, so provide/inject are type-checked.

questions.prompt: How can you let descendants read shared state but not directly mutate it?

options.text: Provide it wrapped in readonly() and expose functions for controlled updates

questions.explanation: Wrapping the state in readonly() before providing prevents descendants from reassigning it; provide separate functions to make controlled changes.

questions.prompt: When is a Pinia store a better fit than provide/inject?

options.text: For a single value shared within one subtree
For app-wide shared state used across many unrelated parts of the app

questions.explanation: provide/inject shines for a subtree's context; app-wide state that many unrelated components share is usually cleaner in a Pinia store.
